Guides

Introducing allergens

Delaying peanut, egg, and milk doesn’t prevent allergy. For most babies, the safer plan is to start them in a safe texture and keep them coming.

Key points

Start the common allergens when you start solids. For most babies that’s around six months, and never before four.
Regular peanut from infancy sharply reduced peanut allergy in high-risk children. In the LEAP trial, children with severe eczema or egg allergy had a relative reduction of about 80 percent by age five.
Some babies should only try peanut once a doctor agrees. That means babies with severe eczema, an existing egg allergy, or both. If your doctor is worried, don’t go ahead on your own.
Redness around the mouth isn’t anaphylaxis. Trouble breathing, floppiness, hives all over, or repeated vomiting after a food is an emergency.

What the evidence says now

For years, families were told to delay peanut, egg, and fish. Allergy rates kept rising under that advice, and it didn’t bring them down. ESPGHAN now says allergenic foods can be introduced when solids begin, any time after four months. For a healthy baby, in practice that means when solids start, around six months.

The foods worth planning for are peanut, egg, cow’s milk, wheat, sesame, fish, soy, and tree nuts. Shellfish can join the list once you’re ready to serve it fully cooked and finely chopped. Offer them as real food, not a hidden trace, and keep serving them.

LEAP, EAT, and the guidelines that followed

LEAP enrolled babies at high risk because of severe eczema, egg allergy, or both. Those who ate peanut regularly until age five were far less likely to develop peanut allergy than those who avoided it. The EAT trial offered six allergens from three months to breastfed babies from the general population. The protection was clearest in children who actually ate the foods often enough, which many families found hard to manage.

The US addendum guideline put LEAP into practice: for high-risk babies, peanut is considered between four and six months, once other solids show the baby is ready, often after testing. Babies with mild or moderate eczema are offered peanut around six months. Babies without eczema can have it along with everything else. European guidance points the same way.

The first tastes

Choose a morning when your child is well, not a vaccination day or a day with a fever. Offer a small amount of one new allergen and stay close. For peanut, the right texture is smooth peanut butter thinned into yogurt or fruit. A spoonful of thick peanut butter can block the airway. Baked egg and hard-boiled egg both count, as long as the white and yolk are set. For sesame, thin tahini into a dip.

If the first taste goes well, repeat it, and then keep it in the weekly routine. Stopping for months after one good taste is how a planned introduction quietly turns into avoidance. A baby with severe eczema or a known egg allergy should be assessed before trying peanut. That’s a doctor’s job, and it may involve a skin test or a supervised feed.

Rashes, illness, and emergencies

Drool plus a new acidic fruit often turns the chin red. That’s contact irritation; it fades and isn’t, on its own, a reason for allergy testing. Spreading hives, swollen lips or tongue, vomiting, a hoarse cry, wheezing, or a baby who turns pale and floppy needs emergency care. Antihistamine is not the treatment for breathing difficulty.

Don’t diagnose an allergy from one meal during an illness, and don’t start a brand-new allergen on a day your child is already unwell. After a true allergic reaction, keep the food out until a specialist has made a plan. Don’t try a challenge test at home.
